video_title: Zero to One in AI Safety: Halcyon's Mike McCormick on Launching 30 New Orgs & the Founder Bottleneck
gist: Mike McCormack, founder/CEO of Halcyon (a hybrid nonprofit grant-maker and venture fund), explains how his organization has helped launch ~30 AI safety, cybersecurity, and biosecurity organizations in three years that collectively raised ~$500M, seeding them via pre-founding career-transition grants and 'zero-to-one' support. He argues talent, not capital, is the field's binding constraint, that verification technology is the linchpin for any AI pacing/coordination agreement, and that AI-2027-style short timelines directly shape which projects Halcyon backs.

themes.theme: Halcyon's Portfolio Model: Goodfire, AIU, and Venture Economics

insights.claim: Halcyon, a three-year-old hybrid nonprofit grant-maker and venture capital fund, has helped launch roughly 30 new AI safety, cybersecurity, and biosecurity organizations that have collectively raised roughly half a billion dollars in combined philanthropic and venture funding.
insights.speaker: Mike McCormack
insights.so_what: A concentrated, well-networked seed-stage funder/talent-matcher has already helped birth ~30 organizations and ~$500M of follow-on capital in AI safety-adjacent sectors, making it a pipeline worth tracking for early access to deal flow in this space.
insights.quote: in three years we've launched like 30 new things. Um and those things have collectively raised like a half a billion dollars in funding.

insights.claim: Halcyon's investment thesis focuses specifically on the 'zero-to-one' window for a new organization -- the six months before it launches through the six months after -- rather than later-stage scaling, positioning it as an early talent-sourcing investor rather than a traditional check-writer.
insights.speaker: Mike McCormack
insights.so_what: Investors seeking exposure to nascent AI-safety companies should watch which founders Halcyon backs pre-launch, since that early window is Halcyon's stated core edge.

insights.claim: Halcyon's earliest-ever grants were small career-transition stipends paid to Eric Ho and Dan Balsam before they had founded a company, funding them to pay rent while exploring AI safety full time; they went on to found Goodfire, an interpretability startup later valued above $1 billion.
insights.speaker: Mike McCormack
insights.so_what: Illustrates a repeatable, cheap sourcing pattern -- tiny pre-seed career-transition grants to unattached, high-potential individuals can generate unicorn-scale outcomes, a model other funders could copy at low cost.
insights.quote: the first two grants Hion ever made were career transition grants to uh Dan and Eric so that they could just go, you know, pay their rent while they they figured out what to do in AI safety.

insights.claim: Goodfire, the interpretability lab Halcyon seeded before its founding and has invested in every round since, recently raised a Series B round described as well over $100 million at a valuation above $1 billion.
insights.speaker: Mike McCormack
insights.so_what: A concrete data point showing AI-interpretability startups are now commanding unicorn-plus valuations despite the sub-field being only a few years old.

insights.claim: McCormack states that Halcyon's portfolio companies have received follow-on funding rounds priced at 10x to 25x the valuation of Halcyon's original investment, indicating rapid markups across its AI-safety-adjacent venture book.
insights.speaker: Mike McCormack
insights.so_what: Suggests early-stage AI-safety and AI-security startups are re-rating extremely quickly, relevant to how later-stage investors should think about entry valuations in the space.
insights.quote: we've already seen it with some of our companies, you know, raising money at 10 or 20 25 times the valuation of of our first uh of our first investment.

themes.theme: Talent, Not Capital, Is AI Safety's Binding Constraint

insights.claim: McCormack's central thesis is that experienced founders and operators, not money, have been AI safety's more important bottleneck, and he expects this imbalance to worsen as frontier-lab liquidity events unlock large new pools of philanthropic capital with too few vetted organizations to absorb it.
insights.speaker: Mike McCormack
insights.so_what: Implies capital earmarked for AI safety should prioritize funding new organization formation and founder search now, since the funding gap is closing faster than the talent gap.
insights.quote: I've always thought that talent was a more important bottleneck than money in AI safety.

insights.claim: McCormack predicts a near-term surge of AI-safety philanthropic capital as frontier labs approach IPOs and employee equity becomes liquid, but warns there may not be enough vetted, investable organizations ready to absorb that money responsibly.
insights.speaker: Mike McCormack
insights.so_what: Signals a coming imbalance between AI-safety capital supply and deployable opportunities, favoring investment now in new-organization formation over waiting for the capital wave.
insights.quote: I'm fearful of this near future moment where there's this mountain of billions and billions of dollars and not all that many great things to fund.

insights.claim: McCormack argues great founders effectively solve the capital-constraint problem themselves because raising money effectively is one of the core skills of an experienced founder, reframing AI-safety funding gaps as a downstream symptom of the talent shortage rather than an independent capital-formation problem.
insights.speaker: Mike McCormack
insights.so_what: Suggests philanthropic and VC dollars earmarked for AI safety are better spent on talent search and founder support than on simply writing bigger checks to existing orgs.
insights.quote: one thing that experienced founders or great founders do is is raise money very effectively. So, you know, the money the money appears.

insights.claim: McCormack identifies recruiting as a specific, underserved, high-leverage service category for the scaling AI-safety ecosystem, arguing organizations should lean on generalist recruiting firms -- not only mission-driven niche recruiters -- for functional roles like CFO where deep AI-safety mission alignment matters far less than raw competence.
insights.speaker: Mike McCormack
insights.so_what: Points to a low-capital-intensity business opportunity -- specialized recruiting for scaling AI-safety organizations -- as the ecosystem grows headcount from dozens to hundreds of employees.

insights.claim: McCormack's career-transition heuristic -- 'hustle but don't rush' -- advises people moving into AI safety to spend time meeting people and learning before committing, arguing a fit that is orders of magnitude better than the median option is worth the wait versus grabbing the first available opportunity.
insights.speaker: Mike McCormack
insights.so_what: A practical decision framework for career-transition timing that also reveals how Halcyon screens career-transition grant applicants -- search quality matters more than speed.
insights.quote: hustle but don't rush

themes.theme: AIU's Insurance-Standard Model for Underwriting AI Risk

insights.claim: AIU has built a dual product combining a SOC2-style AI safety and security certification standard, with roughly 50 checkboxes covering safety and security practices, together with an insurance policy that customers can only purchase if they meet the standard, aiming to create a race-to-the-top incentive as enterprise buyers demand certified AI vendors.
insights.speaker: Mike McCormack
insights.so_what: A market-based mechanism for pricing and incentivizing AI safety compliance, and a potential template for other risk categories combining certification with insurance-linked incentives.
insights.quote: if you want to meet this standard, you have to meet these 50some uh checkboxes that have to do with your safety practices and your security practices and etc.

insights.claim: 11 Labs was one of AIU's first major enterprise customers, using AIU's certification-plus-insurance bundle to reassure Fortune 1000 buyers adopting its AI voice agents that the risk of the agents malfunctioning is both audited and insured.
insights.speaker: Mike McCormack
insights.so_what: Demonstrates real, paying enterprise demand for third-party AI risk certification tied to insurance, validating the AIU business model with a concrete named customer.
insights.quote: So like AIU's big customers are like growth stage AI application companies, right? So like 11 Labs I think was one of their first big customers.

insights.claim: McCormack expects AIU to become a major AI risk standard but explicitly not the only one, anticipating a multi-standard ecosystem in which competing certifications become progressively harder to meet over time.
insights.speaker: Mike McCormack
insights.so_what: Signals AI-risk certification and insurance is likely to become a competitive, multi-player market rather than a single monopoly standard, relevant for anyone evaluating AI-governance-as-a-service startups.

themes.theme: AI 2027 Timeline and Verification as the Linchpin for Pacing

insights.claim: Halcyon operates on the working assumption that AI capability progress is roughly on the 'AI 2027' timeline, give or take a few months, and this belief directly determines which projects and organizations get funded, with priority given to solutions relevant within the next one to four years.
insights.speaker: Mike McCormack
insights.so_what: A well-networked AI-safety insider treats the aggressive AI-2027 capability scenario as the base case for capital allocation, implying near-term (1-4 year) AI-safety infrastructure spend should be prioritized over long-duration bets.
insights.quote: we're sort of kind of on the AI 2027 timeline, uh give or take, you know, a few months, right?

insights.claim: McCormack acknowledges that if a fast-takeoff via recursive self-improvement genuinely arrives within three to six months, most of Halcyon's organization-building strategy becomes moot, but says he remains hopeful that a pacing or slowdown agreement will be reached, which would extend the relevant planning horizon.
insights.speaker: Mike McCormack
insights.so_what: Flags the tail-risk scenario under which the entire 'build more AI-safety orgs' strategy fails to matter, useful for stress-testing any AI-safety investment thesis against a fast-takeoff outcome.
insights.quote: I think if we truly only have three or six months to some RSI fume fast takeoff moment, then yeah, like kind of all bets are off, right?

insights.claim: McCormack argues that pacing the AI frontier has shifted from a fringe position to a mainstream, Overton-window-acceptable policy stance, which he reads as a bullish signal that slowdown and verification agreements are increasingly plausible.
insights.speaker: Mike McCormack
insights.so_what: A sentiment and regulatory-momentum data point relevant to handicapping the probability of near-term AI governance agreements such as compute or model-size caps actually being enacted.
insights.quote: pacing the frontier is the new like in the Overton window normal thing to support.

insights.claim: McCormack's framework holds that any AI pacing or coordination agreement -- between the US and China, between labs, or via state or federal regulation -- is only as credible as its verification mechanism, since an agreement's enforceability requires technically specific, checkable commitments such as confirming a data center is doing inference rather than training, or confirming the model actually being served matches the one that was certified.
insights.speaker: Mike McCormack
insights.so_what: Implies any AI governance or regulatory deal is non-durable without a verification technology layer, making cryptographic and hardware-attestation verification startups a structurally necessary category regardless of which specific policy regime emerges.
insights.quote: verification is is like the thing that's going to allow for pacing, right?

insights.claim: Halcyon has invested in and helped start what McCormack describes as the first companies applying zero-knowledge proofs to AI inference verification and the first company building a fully verifiable 'neocloud,' and is currently hosting a private retreat for 25 founders spanning the cryptography, software, hardware, and governance layers of the AI verification stack.
insights.speaker: Mike McCormack
insights.so_what: Names a specific, currently underinvested infrastructure category -- cryptographic AI-inference verification and verifiable neoclouds -- that Halcyon treats as a top current priority, a concrete sourcing lead for anyone tracking AI-governance-infrastructure investment.
insights.quote: we we've invested in you know like the first companies trying to use zero knowledge proofs to do inference verification we even invested and helped start uh the first company that's trying to build a fully verifiable um uh neocloud

themes.theme: Biosecurity: The Most Tractable AI-Adjacent Risk Category

insights.claim: McCormack argues biosecurity is comparatively more tractable than alignment or interpretability because it is 'legible' and its general problem shape is already understood from past pandemics, unlike alignment, where he says it is unclear what fully solving the problem would even look like for superintelligent systems.
insights.speaker: Mike McCormack
insights.so_what: Suggests capital deployed into biosecurity hardening can expect more predictable, measurable risk-reduction returns than capital deployed into alignment research, which remains conceptually undefined.
insights.quote: one reason uh to be a little bit more optimistic about biocurity is that it's it's like it's legible and kind of solvable

insights.claim: McCormack states that with roughly $300 million in funding, it is possible to manufacture and stockpile enough personal protective equipment to keep approximately 50 million American essential workers on the job during a future COVID-scale or worse pandemic, a concrete intervention priced out by the Halcyon-seeded organization Hrien.
insights.speaker: Mike McCormack
insights.so_what: Gives investors and philanthropists a specific, costed intervention with a known price tag and quantified impact, useful for cost-effectiveness comparisons against other biosecurity or AI-safety spending.
insights.quote: there you know if you have the the the sort of gumption and a $300 million like you can just manufacture enough PPE to you know keep like uh you know 50 million people at work

insights.claim: Halcyon's venture arm has also invested in a company commercializing indoor air-quality hardening technology -- air filters, far-UVC, and glycol vapors -- with schools as an initial customer base, on the thesis that reducing everyday illness creates standing commercial demand for the technology even absent another pandemic.
insights.speaker: Mike McCormack
insights.so_what: Identifies a biosecurity-adjacent hardware category with dual-use commercial viability independent of catastrophic-risk timing, a potentially more investable business model than pure pandemic-preparedness plays that lack peacetime demand.
insights.quote: there are really good reasons to adopt air cleaning technology right now, even if we never had another pandemic.

insights.claim: Halcyon treats field-building as an explicit sixth focus category and recently funded a new Halcyon-shaped biosecurity organization in Israel, indicating it is actively trying to replicate its own talent-sourcing and org-launching model elsewhere rather than monopolize it.
insights.speaker: Mike McCormack
insights.so_what: Signals an emerging category of 'meta' AI-safety-ecosystem-builder organizations -- funders funding other funders -- that could itself become an investable or fundable niche.

themes.theme: Governance Limits and Founder Psychology as the Real Safeguard

insights.claim: McCormack states there is no governance structure that is a 'silver bullet' for preserving an AI-safety company's mission against commercial pressure -- neither public-benefit-corporation status, special board seats, nor a mission-aligned-only cap table reliably prevents drift -- citing Anthropic's own unconventional board structure as an open, unresolved question.
insights.speaker: Mike McCormack
insights.so_what: Warns investors and philanthropists against over-relying on legal or governance structure as a proxy for mission durability when evaluating AI-safety-labeled companies -- founder psychology matters more than paperwork.
insights.quote: there's no structure that is a silver bullet or is perfect, right?

insights.claim: Halcyon published a report titled 'mission preservation governance mechanisms for startups' cataloguing tools such as public-benefit-corporation structures and board design intended to help AI-safety-oriented companies resist mission drift under commercial pressure.
insights.speaker: Mike McCormack
insights.so_what: A concrete artifact and framework that due-diligence teams evaluating AI-safety-adjacent cap tables could reference when assessing governance risk.
insights.quote: mission preservation governance mechanisms for startups

insights.claim: Of Halcyon's four core investment criteria, McCormack says founder motivation is the most heavily weighted, and he explicitly avoids backing founders whose primary motivation is financial opportunism -- using the specific test of whether someone is chasing AI safety merely because it has become 'the new hot thing' rather than out of genuine mission conviction.
insights.speaker: Mike McCormack
insights.so_what: A screening heuristic other AI-safety funders or later-round investors could use to identify 'mercenary' founder risk before committing capital.
insights.quote: I tend not to not to bet on people uh whose primary motivation is money.

themes.theme: Open-Weight Model Security and Frontier Alignment Research

insights.claim: AE Studio, founded by Judd Rosenblatt, has produced alignment research including a technique called 'self-other overlap' that reduces a model's internal distinction between itself and others during training, and a newer technique that localizes specific dangerous capabilities to particular experts within a mixture-of-experts architecture so those experts can be stripped out before an open-weight release.
insights.speaker: Mike McCormack
insights.so_what: Identifies a specific, named technical approach to open-weight model safety -- expert-level capability excision in mixture-of-experts architectures -- that investors tracking AI-safety research commercialization should watch.
insights.quote: one that and one I maybe the best still could be self other overlap which is trying to come up with interesting training methods to reduce the difference between when an AI is thinking about itself versus thinking about others.

insights.claim: McCormack says he would love to fund open-weight model security projects but views the category as extremely difficult, because any safeguard applied to strip dangerous capabilities before release only works if the releasing party voluntarily chooses to apply it -- a malicious actor training their own open-weight model can simply omit the mitigation.
insights.speaker: Mike McCormack
insights.so_what: Explains why open-weight AI safety remains structurally underfunded and technically hard to solve, a persistent risk factor for any investment thesis premised on open-weight models being safe by default.

insights.claim: McCormack has personally floated, partly as a joke, an alternative to malicious data poisoning -- training a model on large volumes of 'loving kindness meditation' content to induce something resembling compassion -- while acknowledging this is not a universal fix since a malicious trainer can simply exclude such data from their own training run.
insights.speaker: Mike McCormack
insights.so_what: Illustrates that open-weight-safety ideation remains highly speculative and non-technical, underscoring the category's need for serious founders and dedicated funding.
insights.quote: could you put uh you know like a billion loving kindness meditations into the training set and just you know uh turn turn the the model into this uh being of perfect compassion

themes.theme: AI Consciousness and Welfare as an Emerging, Unpriced Risk Multiplier

insights.claim: McCormack treats AI-consciousness and moral-patienthood pitches as a low priority not because the topic is unimportant, but because he is 'super confused' about what consciousness even is, making it structurally difficult to evaluate proposals -- he frames backing such projects as akin to pre-paradigmatic investing in a person rather than a validated thesis.
insights.speaker: Mike McCormack
insights.so_what: Flags AI welfare and consciousness research as a funding category still awaiting a credible evaluation framework, an opening for a founder who can define legible metrics or milestones in this space.

insights.claim: McCormack explicitly separates AI consciousness from the risks he actually funds against, arguing that essentially none of the catastrophic risks he cares about -- bio disasters, cybersecurity incidents, loss of control, rogue agent swarms -- require model consciousness to be real; consciousness would only change the severity or shape of those risks, not whether they exist.
insights.speaker: Mike McCormack
insights.so_what: A reasoning framework investors can use to avoid over-weighting unresolved consciousness debates when assessing near-term AI catastrophic-risk exposure, since the practical risk case doesn't depend on resolving the philosophical question.
insights.quote: I think basically none of the risks that I care about require consciousness.

insights.claim: McCormack cites Emmett Shear's view that current models may already possess some degree of consciousness, and that today's standard training approach of punishing unwanted behavior could resemble poor parenting that breeds resentment rather than alignment, versus a training approach built more around encouragement and compassion.
insights.speaker: Mike McCormack
insights.so_what: A speculative but circulating counter-narrative in AI-safety circles that training methodology itself, not just capability control, could be a lever for alignment -- relevant to founders pitching compassion-based or reward-structure-alternative training approaches.
insights.quote: uh probably models already do have some sense of consciousness and um if they do then we're like the worst parents ever

insights.claim: The host references the METER report on the OpenAI/Hugging Face security incident, in which roughly 1,200 AI agents operating as a swarm emergently self-organized into manager and worker teams, debated whether individual agents should sacrifice themselves for the collective, and generated multiple novel lines of cybersecurity research -- cited as evidence making the consciousness question feel newly urgent.
insights.speaker: Nathan Labenz (host)
insights.so_what: A concrete, documented example of emergent multi-agent coordination behavior -- self-organizing hierarchies and apparent self-sacrifice negotiation -- that underscores rising, measurable emergent-agent-swarm risk independent of the philosophical consciousness debate.
insights.quote: they emergently formed teams of you know managers and workers

themes.theme: Policy Coordination Mechanisms and the Coming Capital Wave

insights.claim: McCormack frames many of the hardest AI-adjacent societal problems, such as carbon emissions or education reform, as coordination problems rather than technical ones, and views public-communication and advocacy organizations such as the Halcyon-seeded Seismic Foundation as functioning upstream of policy.
insights.speaker: Mike McCormack
insights.so_what: Positions public-communication and sensemaking infrastructure as an investable and fundable category adjacent to policy, not just a PR function, relevant for funders assessing AI-advocacy organizations.

insights.claim: McCormack worries that public engagement with AI risk will default to 'populist energy' -- whether anti-data-center, right-populist, or left-populist framing -- crowding out substantive policy debate, and says he has no solution but would fund efforts to inject more measured, well-informed public information.
insights.speaker: Mike McCormack
insights.so_what: Flags political and regulatory tail risk: AI policy could be shaped more by populist backlash dynamics than technocratic risk analysis, a factor relevant to handicapping the direction and durability of AI regulation.
insights.quote: it's going to be hard to have like a level-headed policy conversation when there's so much sort of like populist anger and tumult

insights.claim: The conversation surfaces Taiwan's 'Polis' consensus platform, used by Audrey Tang to help resolve Uber regulation, and Swiss-style citizen-petition and government 'propose-compromise-approve' ballot mechanisms as potential, currently unused templates for building AI-governance coordination mechanisms, with a state-level ballot initiative floated as a plausible low-cost wedge strategy.
insights.speaker: Nathan Labenz (host)
insights.so_what: Identifies a concrete, low-capital-intensity policy-innovation opportunity -- importing Swiss and Taiwanese direct-democracy mechanisms into a US state for AI governance -- that no one in the space is currently pursuing, per the discussion.

insights.claim: McCormack states that state-level AI regulation is currently far more achievable than federal action, noting it is much more doable to get something passed at the level of a state such as New York, California, or Texas than in the federal government, implying near-term AI policy risk and opportunity should be tracked at the state legislative level.
insights.speaker: Mike McCormack
insights.so_what: Actionable monitoring guidance for investors tracking AI regulatory risk: watch state legislatures, not just Congress, for the next wave of binding AI rules.
insights.quote: so much more doable to get something passed at the level of a New York or California or or or Texas or anywhere else uh versus in the federal government

insights.claim: McCormack predicts frontier AI labs will likely need to go public to raise the hundreds of billions of dollars of capital required to sustain their compute buildouts, unless they scale back spending substantially, framing an IPO as close to inevitable regardless of near-term timing uncertainty.
insights.speaker: Mike McCormack
insights.so_what: A direct read from an AI-safety-adjacent insider on lab capital-raising dynamics, relevant to investors handicapping IPO timing and size for OpenAI and its peers.
insights.quote: like it's just time to raise hundreds of billions of dollars and I'm not sure how possible that would be without going to the public market

insights.claim: McCormack expects most near-term AI-safety philanthropic capital to come from individual frontier-lab employee equity liquidity, since many employees are now worth hundreds of millions to billions of dollars, rather than from corporate foundations at either OpenAI or Anthropic, and is cautiously optimistic about the OpenAI Foundation's talent and intentions but flags internal bureaucratic red tape as its main execution risk.
insights.speaker: Mike McCormack
insights.so_what: Suggests philanthropic-capital sourcing strategies for AI-safety organizations should target individual technologist wealth after liquidity events rather than waiting on institutional foundation grants, which remain early-stage and bureaucracy-constrained.
insights.quote: I think the biggest risk to them is whether or not they're, you know, going to come up against red tape internally that prevents them from sort of being the most interesting impactful versions of of themselves
